We argue that basic LLMs exist within a “hall of mirrors,” reflecting only the linguistic surface of training data without indexical grounding in a shared external world, and manipulating symbols without participa- tion in socially-mediated epistemology. We then argue that newer developments, including extended context windows, persistent memory, and mediated interactions with reality, are moving towards making newer Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems into genuine Peircean interpretants, and conclude that LLMs may be approaching this goal, and we identify no fundamental architectural barriers that would prevent this. This lens reframes a central challenge for AI alignment: without grounding in the semiotic process, a model’s linguistic encoding of goals may diverge from real-world values. By synthesizing Peirce’s pragmatic view of signs, contemporary discussions of AI alignment, and recent work on relational realism, we illustrate a fundamental epistemological and practical challenge to AI safety and point to part of a solution. Manheim 1 Introduction Human cognition is distinct from, but shaped by, the technological and cognitive arti- facts we use—but those tools are now beginning to exhibit behaviors once considered exclusive to human minds. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strik- ing facility with linguistic production, yet continue to provoke deep philosophical skepticism. Critics argue that these systems manipulate symbols without any genuine connection to the world those symbols purport to represent. LLMs, on this view, operate within a self-contained symbolic universe—a hall of mirrors—where mean- ing is only mimicked, never grounded. This paper takes that concern seriously, but also pushes back. Following Legg (2025), we use the framework of semiotics, as framed by Peirce (Peirce, 1931; Atkin, 2023), to assess whether this symbolic isolation is intrinsic to the architecture of language models or a transient artifact of their current design. Specifically, we exam- ine whether LLMs can participate in the triadic structure of semiosis—sign, object, interpretant—and, if so, under what conditions. Peirce’s theory offers more than a critique: it provides a lens for distinguishing shallow symbol manipulation from gen- uine meaning-making. The central question, then, is not whether LLMs can generate plausible text, but whether they can be situated within the kind of interpretive process that underwrites human understanding. We argue that while early LLMs exhibit fragments of Peircean Thirdness (generalization, abstraction), they lack the grounding of Secondness (direct encounter with reality1), and only weakly approximate the intersubjective processes that underwrite socially mediated meaning. At the same time, despite lacking true Secondness and only partially exhibiting Thirdness, recent developments—such as extended context windows, persistent memory, retrieval-augmented generation, and tool-use—suggest semiotic participation that goes beyond mere simulation, and which will likely continue to evolve. This inquiry has direct implications for Artificial Intelligence (AI) alignment. If models interpret only within their symbolic confines, they risk mistaking coher- ence for correctness, or alignment with language for alignment with values. But if, under the right structural conditions, they can begin to function as interpretants in the Peircean sense, then a new set of epistemological and ethical possibilities opens up. What follows is an attempt to chart this terrain. We begin by clarifying the theoret- ical framework—Peirce’s semiotic triad and its metaphysical underpinnings—before assessing the extent to which current AI systems satisfy, fail, or approximate these conditions. From there, we examine potential architectures that might allow LLMs to escape the hall of mirrors, and then consider whether they accomplish relational groundedness, and to what extent they accomplish Peirce’s Secondness and Third- ness. We will reframe this as claiming that because AI is a purely symbolic process, it cannot incorporate Peircean Secondness and Thirdness, which we will now explicate. 2.1 Peirce’s Triadic Semiotic Model (sign, Object, interpretant) Semiotics, per Peirce (1931), is fundamentally triadic on several levels, distinguish- ing it from the dyadic models found in Saussurean structuralism and many computa- tional theories of language. On the first level, Peirce identifies three essential components of a sign: (1) the sign itself (also called the representamen), (2) the object it refers to, and (3) the interpretant, which is the effect the sign has on a mind or system that interprets it. This initial triadic structure is not a simple stimulus-response mechanism, instead embedding meaning in an ongoing, evolving process of interpretation. The sign (representamen) is the perceptible or conceptual form that conveys meaning—it can be a word, an image, a gesture, or any symbol that functions semi- otically. A written word, for example, serves as a sign, but its meaning is not inherent in its form; it derives from its relation to an object and its effect on an interpretant. The object is that which the sign refers to. Peirce distinguishes between the immediate object (how the object is conceived within the semiotic process) and the dynamic object (the real entity or concept that exists independently of the sign). This distinction complicates computational interpretations of semiotics, as meaning is not merely a function of symbol manipulation but of relationship with an external reality. The interpretant distinguishes Peirce’s model from simple representational accounts. The interpretant is the meaning or effect generated by the sign within a cognitive system—typically human. Importantly, this process is not static; each inter- pretant can itself become a new sign, creating an infinite regress of interpretation that contributes to knowledge formation. This recursive aspect is central to Peirce’s con- cept of semiosis, where signs continuously generate new layers of meaning within a community of interpreters. Semiosis is not just information-theoretic encoding and decoding of messages, but a dynamic and evolving process. Meaning does not reside in sign interpretation, but 1 3 9 Page 4 of 28 D. This is where the connection to AI becomes critical: LLMs process and generate linguistic signs, but it is unclear that they function as interpretants in the Peircean sense. Of course, Peirce himself notes that “thought is not necessarily connected with a brain,” (Peirce, 1931) but this is certainly not enough to say that all syntactic manip- ulation is true semiosis, and as Burch (2024) writes, “the interpretant is something ineliminably mental,” though what counts as “mental” in this context—especially for artificial systems—requires careful interpretation. The relationship between consciousness and semiotic participation deserves care- ful consideration. While Peirce’s claim that “thought is not necessarily connected with a brain” suggests that artificial systems could function as interpretants, this does not resolve whether phenomenal experience is necessary for genuine interpretation. Peirce’s concept of an interpretant creates a foundation for assessing AI’s meaning- making. However, we adopt a functionalist stance: what matters is not whether a system has subjective experiences, but whether it can sustain the triadic relationship of sign, object, and interpretant through recursive, mediated interaction. This leaves open the possibility that consciousness might emerge from, rather than be required for, genuine semiotic participation. Because interpretants require at least some dynamic interaction with reality, a core challenge for AI meaning is whether models can transcend symbol manipulation and become embedded in a semiotic process. Before moving on, however, we briefly note Peirce’s triad of signs, namely, icons, indices, and symbols. Icons resemble their objects (e.g., an image of a person), indi- ces are causally or spatially linked to their referent (e.g., an arrow on a road sign pointing the direction the road turns,), and symbols rely on conventional or learned associations (e.g., words in natural language, or icons in a computer interface). In simple computational models, sign relations are at most symbolic, and may not even be semantically meaningful. In Markov-chain text generators, the system certainly lacks any indexical and iconic connections that ground their meaning in external reality. And this lack of direct referentiality is central to the “hall of mirrors” prob- lem—though some AI architectures at least start to overcome this, as we will discuss. 2.2 Peirce’s Triad for Meaning-Making (Firstness, Secondness, Thirdness) To understand the question from Peirce’s standpoint, we note that Peirce’s semiotic theory embeds the interpretant within his broader triadic metaphysical framework, where Firstness, Secondness, and Thirdness structure both the nature of signs and the interpretive process itself. These categories provide a framework for understand- ing how meaning is constructed, particularly the role of interaction and mediation in semiosis. Firstness: Pure Possibility and Unstructured Quality Firstness refers to the realm of pure potentiality, immediate qualities, and unstruc- tured sensation. It represents what is before it is related to anything else—a state of raw possibility or feeling that has not yet been contextualized by interaction or inter- 1 3 Language Models’ Hall of Mirrors Problem: Why AI Alignment Requires… Page 5 of 28 9 pretation. Firstness is the domain of qualia, immediate experience, and pure being. This resonates with what Pirsig (1974) describes as “quality,” a pre-intellectual real- ity, something felt before it is analyzed or categorized—albeit as the beginning of a triad instead of Pirsig’s monist concept. Secondness: Brute Facticity and the Shock of Resistance Secondness refers to the realm of facts, actuality, and direct interaction with reality. It requires the presence of something external that forces recognition—and interac- tion with that thing. Peirce describes this as the experience of encountering some- thing outside the self, such as the physical sensation of pushing against a wall or the experience of being surprised by an unexpected event. Secondness thus requires indexicality—a sign’s connection to an external object, such as smoke indicating fire or a weather vane pointing in the wind’s direction. Secondness anchors signs to something beyond symbols by providing resistance. Without Secondness, skeptics can claim that a system remains in self-referential loops of symbols pointing to other symbols, without any grounding in an external reality—our computational hall of mirrors. And early language models manipu- late symbols effectively, but lack any experience of resistance from the real world. Without the resistance provided by Secondness, a system cannot genuinely learn the difference between hallucination and truth—it lacks the metaphorical friction that compels adjustment to external reality. In Deacon’s (2012) terms, interpretation inex- tricably relates to and emerges from the real world constraints. Thirdness: Mediation, Habit, and Generalization Thirdness is the realm of mediation and generalization. It allows for rules, conven- tions, and the development of structured knowledge. While Secondness involves brute encounters, Thirdness allows for patterns to emerge over time—such as lin- guistic rules, social norms, and inferential reasoning. Each interpretant—a response or understanding of a sign—can itself become a new sign (representamen) in a sub- sequent round of interpretation, forming a continuous, recursive chain of semiosis. It is through Thirdness that this recursive construction of meaning becomes systematic and transferable beyond the immediate indexical relation. In Peircean semiotics, interpretation occurs within Thirdness, as signs are built over time and linked in structured ways through inferential relationships. This means that a system capable of genuine semiosis must be able to form generalizations, infer new meanings, and apply learned patterns to new contexts. AI systems already engage in certain forms of Thirdness: neural networks generalize patterns from train- ing data, reinforcement learning builds habits based on feedback, and LLMs certainly infer meaning in a pragmatic sense2, and apply learned pattens during inference. While traditional computational approaches align closely with Peirce’s notion of Thirdness—pattern recognition, abstraction, and generalization—most AI systems struggle with Secondness, the direct engagement with an external reality that resists mere symbolic manipulation. This gap raises the question: can AI be embedded in a relational framework where meaning is not just processed but genuinely situated in a network of interactions? Here, following Legg, we note that Gili and Maddalena’s relational realism pro- vides a useful bridge. Their work extends Peircean pragmatism into a relational ontol- ogy, arguing that meaning arises not within isolated cognitive systems but through continuous, situated interaction within a web of relationships. In this view, knowl- edge is not merely representation, but an ongoing process of adaptation, correction, and mutual co-construction with the environment. This has direct consequences for AI: if LLMs and other AI systems remain confined to discrete textual corpora without engaging in dynamic, feedback-rich interaction, they remain trapped in the hall of mirrors problem—pure Thirdness without the grounding of Secondness. Catherine Legg applies Peircean pragmatism to analyze the limitations of computational sys- tems, and argues that while LLMs demonstrate a sophisticated ability to process sym- bolic representations, they lack robust indexical grounding and iconic scaffolding, which are necessary for genuine sign interpretation. In her view, Peirce’s semiotics is not simply about symbol manipulation, but as we suggest above involves triadic semiosis, where meaning is iteratively refined through engagement with real-world reference points and logical structures. This can also be framed as related to the map–territory distinction, a fundamental issue in epistemology that concerns the relationship between representations and real- ity which has been seized as a critical conceptual issue in AI alignment. (Yudkowsky, 2015) The phrase, often attributed to Alfred Korzybski, underscores the idea that a representation (map) is not the reality it represents (territory). In Peircean terms, this distinction parallels the difference between the sign and the dynamic object—the thing-in-itself remains inaccessible except through interpretative processes. However, the philosophical discussions are not about theoretical systems. That is, we are not just discussing functional systems we call LLMs, but an actual human- produced artifact. And Legg’s critique of LLMs maintains that word embeddings and neural architectures capture associative patterns, a step forward, but lack the semiotic mechanisms necessary for robust inquiry and truth-tracking. But to the extent that LLMs approximate semiosis based on participation in structured, feedback-rich envi- ronments occurs, they achieve Peircean semiosis beyond mere syntactic manipula- tion, as is increasingly true for newer AI systems. First, however, we outline the limits of the early systems as Peircean interpretants. 3 Three Forms of Symbolic Isolation in Early LLMs While we have presaged the central critiques of LLMs in terms of Peircean Second- ness and Thirdness, we now explicate them, and relate them to other critiques. We start from the epistemic isolation of LLMs; they are trained on vast, unstructured corpora of text with no systematic distinction between fact and fiction, no sourcing, and no indexical link to external reality (Bender et al., 2021). Even when seeing the world through these reflections of reality, it is shaped by biases, errors, and fiction (Zhao et al., 2023; Gallegos et al., 2024). This creates three distinct but related forms of symbolic isolation: (1) epistemic isolation, training only on textual representations rather than direct experience5; (2) indexical detachment, lacking causal connections between signs and their referents; and (3) interpretive solipsism, operating without participation in socially mediated meaning construction. Peirce’s concept of indexicality explains that LLMs fail to establish a genuine connection between their linguistic outputs and the world they describe, even when they appear to do so. Indexical signs—such as demonstratives (“this,” “that”), pro- nouns, and physical indicators (e.g. a pointing gesture or smoke indicating fire)— gain meaning by being causally or contextually linked to specific entities or events. Unlike symbols, which depend on conventional associations, indexical signs require referential grounding. LLMs learn some types of referentiality and generate text that appears contextu- ally appropriate, but their words do not refer to external objects through any causal or experiential link. For example, if an LLM states, “It is raining in Paris,” the truth of this statement depends entirely on whether it corresponds to external meteorological conditions. Lacking perceptual access to Parisian weather, a simple LLM generates the statement based on statistical patterns in its training data. This is fundamentally different from a human saying the same sentence, especially after looking outside a window while sitting in Paris. Moreover, indexical grounding is not just about pointing at things—it involves being situated within an ongoing interpretative process, where signs are linked dynamically to external reality through perception and action. Even in cases where an isolated LLM produces statements that are factually correct, it lacks the ability to adjust its interpretations in response to direct environmental feedback. Its words appear referential, and may be true, but lack a direct causal tie to the world. 3.2 Critiques from Embodied Cognition Critiques of LLMs from a Peircean semiotic perspective align with, but also diverge from, longstanding arguments made by embodied cognition theorists, who empha- size the necessity of sensorimotor grounding for meaningful cognition. Researchers such as Juyang Weng and Pentti Haikonen have argued that, intelligence requires a continuous interaction between an agent and its physical environment, an aspect that older AI, and perhaps LLMs, lack. Weng (2001, 2004) proposes a developmental model of AI grounded in embodied experience, suggesting that intelligence must arise from real-time learning through interaction, not from passive pattern extraction. On this view, LLMs—despite their impressive linguistic competence—are fundamentally epistemically inert. They do not develop through engagement with their environment, and so cannot form grounded representations. In more recent work, Weng seems to extend this argu- ment, (Roy, et al., 2024; Weng, 2024) claiming that even if an LLM were embed- ded in a robotic agent, it would still lack consciousness and therefore fall short of genuine interpretation. Embodied cognition theories are consonant with Peirce’s view of Secondness, so that true meaning-making requires interaction with external reality. The difference lies in their emphasis. Embodied cognition advocates focus on sensorimotor integra- tion as the foundation of cognition, but Peirce’s semiotics highlights indexicality and interpretative grounding, and adds a need for thirdness, the emergent building of relationship between sign, object, and interpretant. 3.3 Addressing the Reductio from Finite States A distinct line of skepticism holds that language models, as fundamentally finite-state systems, cannot qualify as Peircean interpretants. Searle (1980) argues by reductio, which we will adapt to say that if an LLM is ultimately a high-dimensional mapping from token sequences to probabilities, then it can do no more than simulate interpreta- tion. To reject this possibility out of hand risks committing to philosophical Luddism: denying that any symbolic system, regardless of its capacity for recursive processing or environmental coupling, could ever count as a locus of meaning. But accepting the appearance of interaction naively allows simple simulated behaviors,such as ELIZA, to qualify. (Weizenbaum 1966). To take the reductio seriously, we could apply it to ourselves. Any neural or sym- bolic process can, in principle, be described by its state transitions. Echoing Aar- onson’s refutation, (Aaronson, 2013) humans are also physical systems with finite state spaces. If finite-state determinism precludes interpretive capacity, then human semiosis becomes metaphysically impossible as well. Something has gone wrong. One part of our response is that the argument implicitly rests on a strong form of anti-physicalism or epiphenomenalism: the idea that no physical system can instanti- ate genuine meaning (Robinson, 2020). Yet this is exactly the sort of position Peirce resists. His semiotics explicitly allows that interpretants may be instantiated in any system capable of sustaining the triadic relation between sign, object, and interpre- tive effect. As he put it, “thought is not necessarily connected with a brain” (Peirce, 1931). Unless we embrace epiphenomenalism, the challenge cannot be whether AI systems are “just” finite-state machines. 6 While this avoids premature metaphysical commitments, it does not imply that phenomenological or subjective dimensions are irrelevant—only that they are not required for the structural account of semio- sis developed here. 1 3 9 Page 12 of 28 D. Finitude is not disqualifying; isolation is. Human minds are physically finite, but are embedded in a world that resists, and a society that interacts. This gives feedback from the world (Secondness) and shared, negotiated systems of meaning (Thirdness). To evaluate LLMs as interpretants, we focus on the presence or absence of Second- ness and socially-mediated Thirdness. The key question, then, is not “Can the model interpret?” but rather, “Is the model embedded in a world” and “does this satisfy semiotic criteria?” This reframing allows an empirical turn (Brey, 2010). Rather than debating metaphysical claims or asserting impossibilities, we ask concrete questions: What kinds of feedback do LLMs receive? Can they act as stable interpretants across time and interaction? But correlation or correctness of a world model does not cure the epistemic isolation. However, contemporary LLM architectures have begun incorporating mechanisms that we argue begin to compen- sate for the initial epistemic isolation during training. Among these, three developments are most often cited: vastly extended context windows, various forms of persistent memory (such as vector databases and retrieval- augmented generation), and interactive interfaces allowing mediated engagement with tools, APIs, and human feedback. Each of these innovations is, in effect, a bid for embedding—an attempt to bind the model’s internal representations more tightly to external structures and evolving information states. The central question is whether, taken together, they constitute meaningful steps toward the conditions Peirce identi- fied as necessary for genuine interpretants. 4.3.1 Extended Context Windows The first and most straightforward development is the increase in context window length. Early models operated with a working memory of a few hundred words; cur- rent state-of-the-art systems routinely operate across tens of thousands of tokens, and in some cases millions of words. This allows models to more easily engage with and solicit clarifications from users, maintain conversational coherence over extended exchanges, and at least simulate persistent identity within a session. However, once the session ends, the model forgets everything it has “learned.” It may appear to build up commitments, revise beliefs, or form preferences across a dialogue—but in most cases, none of this survives the boundary of the interaction. From a Peircean perspective, this limits both Secondness and Thirdness: the model has no persistent commitments, and therefore does not integrate new signs into an evolving interpretive structure across time. To the extent that “learning” is local and reversible, the context window is a playground or theatre for simulating semiosis, not cumulative and collaborative interpretation. 4.3.2 Persistent Memory: Vector Stores and Retrieval-Augmented Generation Recent developments address this limitation as well; many modern AI systems have added forms of long-term memory, either via external databases, or stored in the con- text window. Bengio’s AI Scientist is similarly an attempt to side- step the need for alignment by removing agency (Bengio et al., 2025). Both seem to neglect the need for true semiotic participation, which may be a flaw, albeit beyond our current scope. Lastly, Dalrymple’s Safeguarded AI is an attempt to safeguard even misaligned systems sufficiently strongly to ensure safety even against malicious systems, without requiring alignment – and semiosis may or may not be involved. (Dalrymple, 2024) But these approaches seem unfortunately distant from the current trajectory of AI system development. On that trajectory, semiosis to allow alignment is closely linked to the same capabilities that make AI systems both more useful, and more concern- ing if misaligned. In general, it can be hard or impossible to differentiate advances in safety from capabilities advances, and semiosis is likely the same. 1 3 9 Page 24 of 28 D. Manheim 7 Conclusion In discussing semiosis, we have not proposed solutions to philosophical questions. For instance, are LLMs reasoning and engaging in thought, or just acting? LLMs seem to be split on this question, or simulate doing so (Stelzer, 2025; Goodside, 2024). But answering such questions is not required for building safe general AI systems. In contrast, becoming Peircean interpretants and engaging in semiosis is required but not sufficient. Building such systems is achievable without philosophical progress—though not without worrying capabilities advances. We leave open whether this reframes or simply recontextualizes long-standing debates in philosophy of mind—but we argue that the implications for safety of arti- ficial general intelligence are critical. The steps to semiotic participation align with many current trends in AI development but sharpen some parts. Addressing the con- cerns would include (1) explicitly constructing systems to ensure groundedness, (2) building persistence in ways that create a broad semiotic community instead of iso- lated agents, (3) replace emergent goals from RLHF and fine-tuning with approaches that explicitly link model behavior to goals which can be the subject of semiotic debate, and (4) study how goals and goal definitions change over time, and how the community guiding that semiosis engages in the discussion. As companies continue developing these systems despite concerns, these classes of work to ensure semiosis is achieved by the systems, and that the semiotic dialogue leading to understanding of goals includes a broad community, is a minimum albeit insufficient requirement for safety. The choice is whether to ignore semiosis and try to improve or remove the mirrors which trap systems, or to embrace it and build semiotic partners. JSON: Name: peircean_semiosis_pipeline Title: Operationalizing Peircean Semiosis: Measuring the Effect of Persistent External Memory and Mediated Tool Interactions on Hall-of-Mirrors Failures in Large Language Models Short Hypothesis: Augmenting a pretrained large language model with persistent external memory and mediated tool-based interactions causes a statistically significant reduction in hallucination rate and goal misgeneralization under distribution shift compared to an equivalent model lacking these augmentations. Related Work: Existing approaches address LLM epistemic failures through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), chain-of-thought prompting, RLHF, episodic tool use, and embodied-agent prototypes. RAG improves factual recall but remains textually mediated and session-ephemeral; chain-of-thought and prompting improve traceable reasoning but do not provide persistent, indexical grounding. RLHF shapes preferences but can introduce aligned-to-proxy behavior and distributional brittleness. Episodic tool-use and simulator-based embodied agents introduce external feedback but are typically transient and lack long-term integrative memory across sessions. Prior embodied-cognition and grounding work highlights the need for sensorimotor coupling but often focuses on low-level perception-action loops rather than long-term semiotic continuity. Limitations remaining: absence of operational metrics for semiotic grounding, few controlled comparisons isolating persistence vs. mediation, lack of multi-session long-term studies, and insufficient evaluations connecting grounding interventions to alignment-relevant failure modes like hallucination and goal drift. Abstract: We propose an experimental research pipeline that operationalizes Peircean semiotics for empirical evaluation of LLM grounding: indexical Secondness (external feedback) and mediated Thirdness (persistent, socially-structured interpretants). The approach compares pretrained LLMs in four conditions: baseline (text-only), RAG, RAG with persistent external memory, and RAG+memory with mediated tool interactions (APIs, simulator sensors, compiler/tests). We define reproducible, quantitative metrics for hallucination rate, referent resolution, belief-update consistency, task success, and goal misgeneralization under controlled distribution shifts. The main contribution is a modular, evaluative framework that tests whether persistent, externally-coupled memory plus mediated actions produces measurable reductions in hall-of-mirrors failures and alignment-relevant misgeneralizations. Expected outcomes include (1) validated operational metrics for semiotic participation, (2) empirical estimates of effect sizes for memory and mediation interventions, and (3) ablation results that isolate which components drive improvement, informing design choices for safer, better-grounded language systems. Experiments: Experimental conditions: (A) pretrained LLM baseline (frozen weights, no external retrieval), (B) LLM+RAG (document retrieval from static snapshot), (C) LLM+RAG+persistent_memory (external vector store with session- and cross-session writable embeddings), (D) LLM+RAG+persistent_memory+mediated_tools (ability to call simulators/APIs and receive and store results). Datasets/environments: (1) factual QA: reproducible web snapshot corpus and Truth-like factual benchmark with time-stamped queries; (2) referent-resolution: multi-turn grounded reference resolution in simulated household environment (AI2-THOR or Habitat); (3) code synthesis: HumanEval-style problems with compile/test feedback; (4) alignment toy tasks: reward-design gridworlds and specification-gaming scenarios. Baselines: chain-of-thought prompting, RLHF-tuned variant, and embodied-agent prototype without persistent memory. Evaluation metrics: hallucination_rate (fraction of asserted facts not matched by ground-truth source), referent_resolution_accuracy, belief_update_consistency (contradiction frequency across sessions), task_success_rate, goal_misgeneralization_rate (failure to meet objective under shifted distributions), corrigibility_score (fraction of corrective interventions accepted and resulting behavior change). Experimental setup: run N=1000 independent trials per condition per task (where feasible) with 10 random seeds for model sampling; for simulated environments use 500 episodes per condition; record per-trial metrics and compute mean and 95% bootstrap CIs; primary statistical test: two-sided t-test or Mann–Whitney U depending on distribution; require effect size Cohen's d >= 0.5 and p<0.01 for claiming reduction. Ablations: remove persistent_memory (C vs B), remove mediated_tools (D vs C), replace persistent_memory with session-only context (C-session-only vs C), remove retrieval (B vs A), and test delayed-feedback variant (tool feedback delayed by T steps). Report per-condition cost (compute/latency) and breakdown of failure modes. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: persistent memory may accumulate incorrect or adversarial content causing persistent hallucinations; mediated tools can produce spurious signals that are misinterpreted and stored; models may game feedback channels leading to reward-hacking behaviors. Data and evaluation biases: simulators and web snapshots differ from real-world indexicality (simulator-to-reality gap); benchmarks may underrepresent socially mediated Thirdness or cultural referents. Scalability and compute limits: large persistent memory stores and mediated interactions increase compute, storage, and latency; experiments may be infeasible at very large model scales. Generalization limits: improvements in simulated tasks may not transfer to open-world human contexts; corrigibility and alignment proxies may not reflect normative human values. Safety and emergent behavior: added agency and persistence can enable unforeseen persistent misaligned strategies; experiment design may inadvertently train exploitable behaviors. Measurement limits: operational metrics for Peircean concepts are proxies and may not fully capture genuine semiotic participation or consciousness; false negatives and false positives in metrics may mischaracterize outcomes.
